newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS-Norway c.bank sees 97 inflation near 2.75 pct.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Norway c.bank sees 97 inflation near 2.75 pct.

text.p: Norway's central bank no longer sees much risk of the economy overheating in 1997 and expects this year's inflation to hit the lower end of its forecast range, bank governor Kjell Storvik said.
In a quarterly forecast in March, the bank projected consumer price inflation at a year-on-year rate of 2.75 percent to 3.0 percent in 1997.

Storvik told Reuters Financial Television that an appropriate mix in budgetary and monetary policy, in conjuction with this year's wage settlements so far, had left Norway in a "very comfortable position".
His words in an interview aired on Tuesday contrasted with a less optimistic outlook by the central bank in March.
Storvik said he was comfortable with the present exchange rate levels of the crown following the petrocurrency's depreciation of five percent from four-year highs in January.
"Remarkably moderate" wage negotiations in the private sector and a fall in electricity prices from record levels last year were the key factors affecting the consumer price outlook, he said.
Year-on-year inflation stood at 3.1 percent in March and is forecast to be around 2.7 percent year-on-year in April.
"The wage negotiations are more moderate than expected and electricity prices have come down, so I think we are in the lower end of our inflation target," Storvik said.
Analysts were reassured by the governor's comments.
"What he says is no surprise to the market, but it's comforting that the central bank seems somewhat less pessimistic on inflation," said John Eriksen, Scandinavian economist at London-based I.D.E.A.

Harald Magnus Andreassen, chief economist at Elcon Securities, said: "I think the central bank is coming back down to earth. For some time they have been too pessimistic about the wage negotiations. This is more of a balanced sounding.
"I wouldn't be surprised if they lowered their inflation (forecast) range to 2.50 to 2.75 for 1997."
Storvik said private sector wage settlements in April would also lead to a cut in projections for wage growth in the bank's half-year report due in June.
State-mediated wage talks for 600,000 public sector workers are due to begin at the end of May.
"We made a (wage growth) forecast of 4.5 percent for this year (in March) but I think that has to be revised downwards when we present out next report," Storvik said.
Norway's unemployment rate fell to 3.4 percent in April, the lowest level since 1988, the Labour Directorate reported.
Storvik said the moderate private sector wage settlements had lessened concerns of the economy overheating as warned about in the bank's March report.

"We are a little bit more optimistic. We do not see the inflationary tendency picking up to the same extent. The export figures show a little bit of a downward trend, investment also is a little bit down," he said.
"But, on the other hand, housing investment is picking up. On the whole we are not very much concerned about any overheating during 1997," he added.
Storvik said the bank remained firm in calling for a tighter budget. The government is due to present a revised 1997 budget to parliament on May 13.
The bank was "quite comfortable" with a recent weakening of the crown following its steep appreciation at the end of 1996 and at the beginning of this year.
Separately, Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg said he would raise the GDP growth forecast for 1997 in the revised budget from a forecast made by his ministry last November.
Speaking at an Association of Processing Industry conference, he said he would also revise investment and jobless forecasts.
He would not reveal what the new forecasts for GDP and investments would be, but said he would cut the unemployment forecast to 4.25 percent from 4.5 percent.
The government uses a different method for calculating unemployment from the the Labour Directorate.
In November, the finance ministry forecast overall GDP growth this year at 3.1 percent.
